title: Contract Review Automation: Top Benefits & Use Cases
summary: Discover the benefits of contract review automation to speed up approvals, reduce legal risk, improve accuracy & free your team for higher-value work.
body_text: Contract review automation is the use of software and artificial intelligence (AI) to systemize and accelerate the contract review process , reducing the amount of manual legal work required to analyze agreements. That efficiency gain is what initially attracts most teams to automation. The 2024 Legal Department Operations Index found that 79% of corporate legal departments were expected to handle higher contract volume without adding headcount. However, even with the pressure becoming impossible to ignore, the 2025 edition of the same report found that only 29% of organizations currently use contract AI for analysis, risk assessment, or due diligence. More importantly, many organizations that have adopted it still admit they’re underusing the technology, which is a significant waste of legal leverage. To help you understand why underusing contract review automation—or ignoring it entirely—is a mistake, this guide breaks down its biggest benefits and most valuable use cases. Key takeaways Contract review automation speeds up legal work By automating repetitive first-pass review, legal teams can review contracts faster, reduce bottlenecks, and return agreements in hours instead of days. AI is best at identifying risks, not replacing legal judgment Modern AI can detect risky clauses, compare contracts against playbooks, and extract key information, but experienced attorneys are still essential for negotiation, strategy, and final approval. The biggest gains come from consistency, compliance, and scalability Automated review applies the same standards to every agreement, helping businesses reduce errors, strengthen compliance, and handle growing contract volumes without expanding legal teams. Contract review automation works best for repetitive, high-volume agreements NDAs, vendor contracts, procurement documents, compliance checks, and contract metadata extraction are some of the workflows where automation delivers the greatest value. The strongest contract review model combines AI with experienced attorneys General Legal pairs AI-powered contract review with elite US-barred attorneys, giving startups faster turnaround, flat-fee pricing, and high-quality legal work without sacrificing human judgment. What is contract review automation? Contract review automation is the practice of using technology to streamline the review, analysis, negotiation, and approval of contracts. Instead of requiring lawyers to manually review every agreement line by line, this approach relies on rule-based systems, workflow automation, and AI to identify key clauses, flag risks, extract critical information, and compare language against internal standards or legal playbooks. In most organizations, contract review automation sits inside the broader Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM) process . CLM covers the entire lifecycle of a contract, from intake and drafting to negotiation, approval, execution, renewal, and ongoing compliance management. Contract review is one of the most important workflow layers inside that system because it determines whether an agreement is safe to execute. So, how does this workflow become automated? How legal teams automate contract review Legal teams automate contract review through several different approaches, depending on contract volume, workflow complexity, and risk tolerance. These include: Rules-based automation: Use predefined templates, clause libraries, and keyword rules to identify standard terms, flag missing provisions, and detect deviations from approved language. This works best for routine, high-volume agreements with predictable language. AI-powered contract review: Use machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) to analyze contracts beyond basic keyword matching. Hybrid review systems: Combine rules-based logic with AI analysis to balance consistency, scalability, and flexibility. Of these three approaches, AI-powered contract review has seen the fastest adoption and the biggest improvements in recent years. Understanding how it works in more detail explains why. How AI-powered contract review works AI-powered contract review begins by converting a contract into machine-readable text. AI models then analyze the agreement contextually rather than relying on keyword detection. This difference matters because rules-based systems depend on predictable language . So, once a clause is substantially rewritten, these traditional systems become less reliable at detecting legal risks. In contrast, AI models can still recognize the same legal meaning, even if the wording changes completely. In addition, the best AI systems improve over time because they learn from historical contracts, negotiation outcomes, redlines, and reviewer behavior. That said, AI is still far better at issue spotting than legal judgment. For example, AI can identify risky indemnity language. However, it can’t reliably decide whether accepting that risk makes strategic sense in the context of a specific customer relationship, deal size, or negotiation dynamic. That decision still requires an attorney. However, most AI-powered contract review tools only handle the first-pass review. After the software flags issues and surfaces risks, your internal legal team still has to interpret the findings, negotiate the agreement, and finalize the redlines. The better model is combining AI review and legal execution in the same system. That’s exactly how General Legal operates. AI agents review contracts first, triaging documents, surfacing risk, summarizing issues, and accelerating analysis, before elite attorneys take over and deliver the final legal work product. The result is faster turnaround, lower operational drag, and a reliable legal review backed by actual human judgment instead of unchecked AI output. Whatever form it takes, contract review automation creates operational benefits across multiple teams. Who benefits from contract review automation? Legal teams benefit most from contract review automation, but they’re rarely the only team waiting on approvals and redlines. In startups, especially, a single contract stuck in review can slow down half the company. The table below breaks down how different teams benefit from contract review automation: Department / Role How contract review automation helps Legal • Reduces repetitive first-pass review work • Accelerates redlining and approvals • Handles higher contract volume Sales • Reduces approval bottlenecks • Accelerates deal cycles • Prevents contracts from stalling late-stage negotiations Procurement • Flags risky vendor terms faster • Standardizes supplier agreements • Increases visibility into vendor obligations Finance • Surfaces payment and renewal terms faster • Reduces invoicing and billing inconsistencies • Supports compliance and audit workflows HR • Streamlines onboarding agreements and NDAs • Reduces policy inconsistencies • Accelerates hiring workflows Founders & executives • Improves deal velocity • Reduces operational drag across teams • Increases visibility into legal and commercial risk ‍ While the specific use cases differ by team, the underlying advantages of contract review automation are remarkably consistent. 8 biggest benefits of contract review automation The eight benefits below explain why companies are replacing manual contract review with automated workflows. 1. It accelerates contract turnaround times According to a 2023 academic study , junior lawyers take an average of 56 minutes to review a legal contract. Review time, however, isn’t the same as turnaround time. That’s because commercial law firms continue to rely on manual workflows. Contracts wait in queues, sit unread in inboxes, move between associates, and cycle through multiple rounds of redline before feedback is returned. Contract review automation removes much of that operational delay. The same study found that the fastest Large Language Model (LLM) outperforms junior lawyers by 77 times in speed, reducing first-pass review from nearly an hour to minutes. Even with a hybrid review approach like the one General Legal offers, contracts are typically returned in hours instead of days or even weeks. 2. It improves contract accuracy and consistency A common criticism of automated systems is that they can make mistakes. However, the same is true of lawyers working through long review queues. As workloads increase, consistency inevitably declines. By contrast, automated systems apply the same review criteria to every agreement , consistently flagging missing protections, outdated clauses, non-standard language, and deviations from internal playbooks. The result is more consistent contract quality, fewer avoidable errors, and lower legal risk. 3. It strengthens compliance and risk management Compliance problems rarely begin with a major legal failure; they stem from small issues that go unnoticed , such as: Outdated indemnity language A vendor agreement that violates internal policy A missing data processing clause Manual review workflows are prone to missing these issues, especially under time pressure. That’s not the case with contract review automation, which creates a more controlled review process by: Analyzing every clause rather than prioritizing only the highest-risk sections Comparing contracts against approved templates, playbooks, and historical agreements to detect deviations Applying automated checks across large contract volumes without sacrificing coverage or consistency 4. It lowers legal operational costs Reducing legal costs is one of the biggest drivers behind contract review automation adoption. The logic is straightforward. Legal teams shouldn’t be paying thousands of dollars for attorneys to keep reviewing the same routine contract issues. Instead, AI systems can handle first-pass review, clause analysis, issue spotting, and document triage in minutes, allowing lawyers to focus on negotiation strategy and higher-risk legal work . 5. It increases visibility into contracts and obligations Many companies have limited visibility into what their contracts contain, where agreements sit in the approval process, and which obligations create legal or commercial risk. Contract review automation changes this by: Centralizing contract data Surfacing key obligations automatically Giving teams real-time visibility into contract status, renewal timelines, risk exposure, and non-standard terms As a result, teams can spend less time searching for information and more time acting on it. 6. It scales legal workflows without adding headcount It’s estimated that a typical Fortune 1000 company manages anywhere between 20,000 and 40,000 active contracts at any given time. Most startups and growing companies never reach that level of contract volume. But even at lower volumes, manual contract workflows become hard to sustain once the business starts scaling . Contract review automation allows businesses to absorb that growth without adding more reviewers and coordinators. That’s because automated systems can process agreements in bulk , automate first-pass review, standardize approval workflows, and route contracts automatically. 7. It improves collaboration across teams Contract review can become increasingly difficult to coordinate as more stakeholders become involved . Without a centralized workflow, the legal department might review one version, sales might edit another, and finance might still approve an outdated draft. Contract review automation addresses this risk by keeping edits, approvals, comments, and redlines synchronized, reducing duplicate work, version conflicts, and coordination mistakes. 8. It allows teams to focus on higher-value work Legal expertise is most valuable when applied to judgment, not repetitive contract administration. By eliminating a huge amount of low-leverage review work , contract review automation allows legal teams to spend more time: Negotiating higher-stakes agreements Evaluating complex legal risks Advising clients on business strategy Handling sensitive commercial decisions Managing difficult counterparties Accelerating critical deals and partnerships In this new division of labor, which tasks actually belong to contract review automation? 7 practical use cases for contract review automation Contract review automation delivers the greatest value when legal teams review large volumes of repetitive agreements under tight deadlines. Some of its most common use cases include: Reviewing NDAs and vendor agreements: High-volume agreements like NDAs , procurement documents, and standard vendor contracts are ideal candidates for automated first-pass review because the same issues tend to appear repeatedly. Handling M&A due diligence and bulk contract analysis : Large-scale contract reviews become substantially more manageable when AI systems can sort, categorize, summarize, and extract key terms from thousands of agreements. Running procurement and sales contract workflows: Faster review workflows help sales, procurement, and operations teams move agreements through approval and signature without constant legal bottlenecks. Comparing contracts against internal playbooks: AI systems can automatically detect deviations from approved legal language, fallback clauses, and company risk standards before agreements are approved. Extracting contract metadata and obligations: Legal teams can pull renewal dates, payment terms, notice periods, and operational obligations from contracts without manually searching through documents. Performing compliance and regulatory checks: AI systems can identify contracts missing required protections or containing language that violates internal policy or regulatory requirements. Identifying risky or non-standard clauses: Contract review automation helps surface problematic language early, reducing the likelihood of risky terms reaching execution. The use cases above make it clear that some tasks are ideal for automation, while others still require judgment. The good news is that you don’t have to choose between the two. The AI-native approach to contract review automation Contract review automation performs exceptionally well on repetitive, standardized review work. As contracts become highly negotiated, strategically sensitive, jurisdiction-specific, or commercially unusual, AI used for automation becomes less reliable. That’s why the strongest contract review workflows aren’t AI-only. They are human-led with AI acceleration —exactly what General Legal offers. We aren’t a legal-tech SaaS company selling software licenses to law firms; we’re an AI-native law firm built for startups and growth-stage companies that need high-stakes legal work delivered with the speed modern businesses expect. Our AI agents handle the repetitive operational layer first before elite US-barred attorneys step in to provide the necessary legal judgment, negotiation strategy, and final review. The result is what most startups want from outside counsel: Contract reviews delivered in hours, not days Flat-fee pricing instead of runaway billable hours Direct access to your lawyer through Slack BigLaw-quality commercial contract work without the operational drag of a traditional firm Support across commercial contracts, employment agreements , vendor and procurement workflows, startup financings, drafting projects, and legal ops workflows If your contract workflows are slowing down growth, it’s probably time to stop relying on fully manual legal operations. Register with General Legal right away to start automating your contract review workflows while keeping real legal judgment where it actually matters. For any questions, reach out directly , and our team will help you determine the right workflow for your business. FAQ How to perform a contract review? Performing a contract review means analyzing an agreement for legal, financial, operational, and compliance risks before signing. Can I use AI to review a contract? An evolved hull works in harmony with MasterCraft’s industry-leading SurfStar System and a substantial 3,800-pound ballast system to deliver powerful, customizable wakes and waves that riders trust from the first pull. Long, clean pockets offer surfers consistent push, while wakeboarders enjoy firm, balanced wakes with crisp transitions. As is the case with all MasterCraft models (other than ProStar), the Rapid Surf presets make setup simple, and Custom Surf controls let riders fine-tune every wave to their preference at all skill levels, combining the familiarity longtime boaters expect with the refinement of a modern X platform. Technology continues to reshape the MasterCraft driving experience, and the X23 is no exception. Matching the X22 and X24, the helm of the X23 features dual panoramic digital displays, intuitive MasterCraft MyDrive controls, keyless ignition and wireless charging for smooth connectivity. Every element is placed with purpose, creating a space that feels polished, functional, and unmistakably X. The cockpit is sculpted, unified, and intentionally laid out to feel open and refined. Deep supportive seating, premium upholstery, and carefully considered proportions create an interior that is both luxurious and inviting. Storage and everyday amenities are seamlessly integrated, with wireless charging, cubbies, cupholders, and speaker grilles blending cleanly into the architecture, while drain channels and solid hardware keep compartments durable and organized over time. The original X23 introduced one of the most loved spaces on the boat: the transom loungers. What began as a thoughtful design decision shaped how crews spend their day and set a new standard in the towboat space. The X23’s iconic transom loungers return, now refined with an oversized design, improved ergonomics and premium materials. Integrated dual rear compartments beneath the seats provide flexible storage, accommodating up to four boards in padded, removable bags or opening up space for bulkier gear. Comfortable, functional, and central to how crews spend the day, this space remains one of the best places to relax on the boat. Design refinement continues throughout the X23 with thoughtful details that elevate both form and function. An evolved pickle-fork bow enhances comfort with deep, secure seating, ergonomic armrests, and a dedicated anchor locker with a hidden cleat to keep mud and moisture out of the interior. Sculpted lines and automotive-level finishes modernize the exterior while maintaining the unmistakable MasterCraft identity. The Z9 tower is fully power-folding and available in seven powder-coat color options, featuring anodized accents, integrated board rack compatibility, SoundPods, and cleanly integrated bimini options for a clean, cohesive aesthetic. Audio performance matches the X23’s elevated design. The all-new SoundStage Audio system, developed in partnership with Meridian, continues to deliver rich, immersive sound with intelligent tuning throughout the cockpit. For riders behind the boat, the optional MAAX transom audio system extends that experience, creating a dedicated sound environment that carries beyond the swim platform. Built-in telematics through MasterCraft Connect provide remote diagnostics, battery management, and system monitoring, ensuring confidence and connectivity alongside industry-leading performance. title: Rimini Street Announces Fiscal First Quarter 2026 Financial and Operating Results
summary: Today, Rimini Street announced its financial & operating results for the fiscal first quarter of 2026. See the highlights for Q1 2026.

Instead, organizations can invest in the modernization of their existing systems by leveraging next generation Rimini Agentic AI ERP solutions that can be quickly and economically deployed over their current ERP and other enterprise software to deliver real competitive advantage.” “We delivered strong first quarter 2026 results that built on second half 2025 momentum, reflecting continued, growing market demand for our differentiated, proven support and innovation solutions,” said Michael Perica, CFO, Rimini Street . “We continued to make additional strategic investments in new AI and innovation offerings to drive growth and further streamlined global operations to provide leverage with scale. Looking ahead, we remain focused on profitable growth, disciplined cost management and a strong balance sheet and cash position. Capital allocation actions in the quarter included a $10 million debt prepayment that reduced outstanding debt to $58.4 million and increased net cash to $73.8 million as of March 31, 2026.” Select First Quarter 2026 Financial Results Revenue was $105.5 million for the first quarter of 2026, an increase of 1.2% compared to $104.2 million for the same period last year; excluding the support services for Oracle’s PeopleSoft software products, revenue increased by 5.2%. As a result, stock-based compensation expense varies for reasons that are generally unrelated to operational decisions in any particular period. Reorganization Costs: The costs consist primarily of severance costs associated with the Company’s reorganization plan. EBITDA is net income adjusted to exclude: interest expense, income taxes, and depreciation and amortization expense. Adjusted EBITDA is EBITDA adjusted to exclude: litigation costs and related recoveries, net, stock-based compensation expense and reorganization costs, as discussed above. In addition, it is also adjusted by unrealized foreign exchange (gains) or losses. Calculated Billings represents the change in deferred revenue for the current period plus revenue for the current period. title: Financial Advisor Magazine: "For Young Adults, Advisors Help Drive Financial Independence"
summary: Pathward's Chief Customer Officer Will Sowell authored a byline in Financial Advisor Magazine exploring how financial advisors can better serve Generation Z as they navigate the complex path from financial dependence to independence.
body_text: Pathward's Chief Customer Officer Will Sowell authored a byline in Financial Advisor Magazine exploring how financial advisors can better serve Generation Z as they navigate the complex path from financial dependence to independence. In the piece, Sowell draws on findings from a recent Pathward report revealing that only 37% of Gen Z respondents consider themselves mostly or completely financially independent from their parents. This gradual path to independence creates unique financial needs that differ significantly from those of older generations. "In many ways, younger adults represent the future of financial services," Sowell writes. "Those who adapt their approach today will be best positioned to serve the next generation of investors, entrepreneurs and wealth creators." The article also explores Gen Z's digital fluency and its implications for the advisor-client relationship. While younger adults expect seamless technology experiences, they still seek trusted expertise for complex financial decisions. Sowell notes that advisors who combine digital convenience with personalized, education-oriented guidance can become stronger partners as their younger clients grow. Read Sowell’s complete article in Financial Advisor Magazine at FA-Mag.com .
